newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global Infotech trade pact on track for approval.
newsitem.headline: Global Infotech trade pact on track for approval.

text.p: A landmark $500 billion pact to scrap tariffs in the booming information technology industry is on track for approval on Wednesday, negotiators said.

The long-awaited global accord, set to benefit customers, manufacturers and world trade, came one step closer to conclusion after the United States, European Union, Canada, Japan, Malaysia and Thailand approved their schedules for tariff cuts in talks late on Tuesday night, trade officials said.
"We're supposed to finish today. There's some work to be done verifying other countries' schedules but I'm hopeful we'll resolve all these issues," said a U.S. negotiator.

Trade officials said 41 countries representing 92 percent of the IT market had committed themselves to the sweeping accord, which analysts say will open the way for a vast expansion of the industry and cut costs for consumers and businesses.
The pact, a big boost to makers of computer and telecoms equipment, will open the way for ambitious future global pacts along with one concluded in February to free up telecom trade.
Washington's trade diplomats said U.S. computer giants IBM, Hewlett Packard, Motorola and Intel were among producers that stood to benefit from an abolition of tariffs.
The accord will also help giant manufacturers in Germany, Japan and South Korea to save tens of millions of dollars and boost overseas earnings, trade officials said.
The accord was originally championed by the United States.

But the list of countries expected to sign up encompasses much of the developing world including the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Israel and Panama, which were to finalise their tariff cut schedules on Wednesday.
The accord, under which the first tariff cuts must take place in July, was shaped in December during a Singapore ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

It cuts tariffs in four stages between 1997 and 2000 in five main product categories: computers, telecom products, semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, software including diskettes and CD ROMs, and scientific instruments.
Foreign ministers of the 15-member European Union formally approved the accord in Brussels on Monday and asked the European Commission to make minor changes to their text and to submit it to the WTO.
Some developing countries will be allowed to delay cuts for some products until after 2000.
One last hurdle was U.S. discontent with EU tariffs on local area network equipment and multimedia personal computers.

Washington says a reclassification of such products by the EU customs authorities has caused higher duties on its imports in violation of world trade rules and has filed a case against the European Union under the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body.
But negotiations were continuing between the EU and Washington to resolve the issue and senior trade officials said it was unlikely to be a deal-breaker.

The United States, European Union and Japan were unhappy with initial offers from key Asian states including Malaysia, Thailand and also India to maintain tariffs on some products until 2005 or 2007 but diplomats said agreement had now been reached on most products.
India, whose high rates concerned Washington, eventually agreed to abolish tariffs by 2000, with those on some products extended until 2005, trade officials said.
"The key thing is that all countries have agreed to bring tariffs on the majority of products down to zero by 2005," said a senior Western trade official.
Although the pact was negotiated outside the WTO framework, it will be incorporated into its rules and signatories will be obliged to extend its terms to all its other members.
